title: UNIT 3: ENZYMES
notes:
✓ Enzymes are mainly protein molecules that act as biological catalysts.

→ They speed up biochemical reactions by lowering activation energy without being consumed.

title: 3.1 WHAT ARE ENZYMES?
notes:
✓ Enzymes are biocatalysts that accelerate chemical reactions by lowering activation energy.

◆ Substrate → molecule acted on by an enzyme.

◆ Active site → region where the substrate binds.

◆ Product → substance formed by the reaction.

◆ Activation energy → minimum energy required to start a reaction.

Enzyme + Substrate → Enzyme–substrate complex → Product + Enzyme.

title: 3.2 PROPERTIES & FUNCTIONS OF ENZYMES
notes:
✓ Enzymes increase reaction rates without changing the nature of the products or being permanently changed themselves.

→ Their activity depends on physical and chemical properties.

title: 3.2.2 FUNCTION OF ENZYMES
notes:
✓ Enzymes bind specific substrates at their active sites and lower activation energy, making reactions occur faster.

◆ Examples:
◆ Amylase → starch → sugars.
◆ Maltase → maltose → glucose.
◆ Lactase → lactose → glucose + galactose.
◆ Trypsin → proteins → smaller products/amino acids.
◆ Lipase → fats → fatty acids and glycerol.
◆ Helicase → unwinds DNA.
◆ DNA polymerase → forms new DNA molecules.
◆ Acetylcholinesterase → breaks down acetylcholine.

title: 3.3 PROTEIN STRUCTURES
notes:
✓ Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. They have four structural levels:

1 Primary → linear amino-acid sequence.

2 Secondary → local folding into α-helix and β-pleated sheet through hydrogen bonding.

3 Tertiary → three-dimensional shape of one polypeptide chain.

4 Quaternary → arrangement of several folded polypeptide subunits.

→ Protein structure determines the shape and function of enzymes.

title: 3.4 ENZYME–SUBSTRATE MODELS
notes: ✓ Enzyme-substrate models explain how a substrate interacts with the enzyme's active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex.

title: 3.4.1 ENZYME–SUBSTRATE BINDING MODELS
notes:
◆ Lock-and-key model → the active site has a shape complementary to the substrate, allowing specific binding.

◆ Induced-fit model → substrate binding causes the enzyme's active site to change shape slightly, improving interaction and catalytic activity.

Lock-and-key = pre-existing fit | Induced fit = shape changes after binding.

title: 3.4.2 ENZYMATIC TRANSITION STATE
notes:
✓ The transition state is the highly activated state reached during an enzyme-catalyzed reaction.

→ The enzyme-substrate complex helps stabilize this state and lowers the energy needed for the reaction.

◆ E = Enzyme | S = Substrate | ES = Enzyme-substrate complex | EP = Enzyme-product complex.

title: 3.5 ENZYME REGULATION
notes:
✓ Enzyme regulation controls enzyme activity according to the needs of the organism.

◆ Allosteric enzymes → have an active site and an additional regulatory/allosteric site. Activators or inhibitors bind to the allosteric site and change enzyme activity.

◆ Covalent modification → chemical groups are added or removed from enzymes to change their activity.

◆ Phosphorylation → addition of a phosphate group; an important regulatory mechanism.

◆ Enzyme inhibition → reduction of enzyme activity by inhibitors.

◆ Reversible inhibition → temporary.

◆ Irreversible inhibition → permanently blocks enzyme activity.

◆ Competitive inhibitor → competes for the active site.

◆ Noncompetitive inhibitor → binds away from the active site and reduces enzyme activity.

◆ Uncompetitive inhibitor → binds to the enzyme-substrate complex.

title: 3.6.1 ENZYME STRUCTURAL CLASSIFICATION
notes:
✓ Simple enzyme → protein component alone and active.

✓ Holoenzyme → complete active enzyme containing:

◆ Apoenzyme → protein part.

◆ Cofactor → non-protein part required for activity.

◆ Coenzyme → loosely attached organic cofactor, often vitamin-derived.

◆ Prosthetic group → firmly attached cofactor, often a metal ion.

Apoenzyme + Cofactor = Holoenzyme.

title: 3.6.2 BASIC CLASSIFICATION OF ENZYMES
notes:
1 Oxidoreductases → catalyze oxidation-reduction reactions.

2 Transferases → transfer functional groups from one molecule to another.

3 Hydrolases → break bonds through hydrolysis.

4 Lyases → break or form bonds without hydrolysis or oxidation.

5 Isomerases → convert molecules into their isomers.

6 Ligases → join two molecules, usually using energy from ATP.

title: 3.7.1 DESCRIPTION OF FACTORS AFFECTING ENZYMATIC ACTIONS
notes:
✓ Temperature → low temperatures slow reactions; excessive heat can denature enzymes.

◆ pH → enzymes have an optimum pH; extreme acidity or alkalinity reduces activity.

◆ Substrate concentration → increasing substrate generally increases reaction rate until available enzyme active sites become occupied.

◆ Enzyme concentration → more enzyme can increase reaction rate when sufficient substrate is available.

◆ Inhibitors → decrease enzyme activity.

◆ Activators → increase enzyme activity.

◆ Radiation → can damage enzymes and reduce their efficiency.

◆ Water → affects enzyme performance when conditions move away from optimum.

◆ End-product inhibition → the final product inhibits an earlier enzyme in a pathway, often by binding to an allosteric site.

title: 3.8 ENZYME KINETICS
notes:
✓ Enzyme kinetics studies the rate of enzyme-catalyzed reactions and the relationship between enzyme, substrate and inhibitor concentrations.

◆ Reaction rate → speed of product formation.
◆ Vmax → maximum reaction velocity.
◆ [S] → substrate concentration.
◆ Km → substrate concentration at half of Vmax.

→ Michaelis-Menten kinetics relates reaction rate to substrate concentration.

title: 3.9.1 USES OF ENZYME APPLICATION
notes:
✓ Cellulase → breaks cellulose for biofuel production.
◆ Ligninase → biomass pretreatment for biofuels.
◆ Protease → removes protein stains; also used in food processing.
◆ Amylase → breaks down starch; used in detergents and food industries.
◆ Lipase → removes fats/oils from laundry and dishware.
◆ Mannanase → removes food stains.
◆ β-glucanase → improves beer filtration.
◆ Papain → tenderizes meat.
◆ Rennin → cheese production.
◆ Trypsin → hypoallergenic baby-food production.
◆ Cellulase + Pectinase → clarify fruit juices.
◆ Nuclease, DNA ligase & polymerase → molecular biology and recombinant DNA work.

title: 3.10.1 STEPS OF MODERN MALTING
notes:
1 Steeping → grain is soaked in water; enzyme activity begins.

2 Germinating → grain sprouts; enzymes break down proteins and carbohydrates and make starch reserves available. The resulting product is green malt.

3 Kilning → germinated grain is heated and dried to stop further germination while developing malt color and flavor.

title: 3.10.2 WHY IS MALTING FOR?
notes:
✓ Malting modifies grain structure and activates enzymes needed for brewing, distilling and food production.

◆ α-amylase + β-amylase → convert starch into simpler sugars such as maltose and maltodextrins.
◆ Yeast → uses simple sugars during alcoholic fermentation.

→ Main purpose → produce enzyme-rich malt for further processing.

notes:

◆ Induced fit → enzyme changes shape after substrate binding.

Protein structures → primary → secondary → tertiary → quaternary.

◆ Inhibitor → decreases activity.
◆ Activator → increases activity.
◆ Holoenzyme = Apoenzyme + Cofactor.

◆ Lyases.
◆ Isomerases.
◆ Ligases.
